questions.q: What is audit "fieldwork," and why does it matter how evidence is gathered beforehand?
options: The fixed window in which an auditor reviews evidence and tests controls — teams that keep evidence current continuously have far less to scramble for than teams who wait
An informal term with no real meaning in a compliance audit
A technical scan run automatically with no human auditor involved
The period after an audit is already complete
questions.explain: Fieldwork is the fixed window an auditor reviews evidence and tests controls in; gathering evidence continuously beforehand avoids scrambling, inconsistent answers, and live-discovered gaps.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an "access log," one of the three real evidence categories in this lesson?
options: AWS CloudTrail event history or Azure Monitor / Activity Log entries showing who accessed what and when
A written incident response policy document
An IAM policy JSON export
A compliance score from Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager
questions.explain: Access logs (CloudTrail, Azure Monitor / Activity Log, sign-in logs) record who accessed a resource and when, separate from configuration exports and written policy documents.

questions.q: What is "stale access," as described in this lesson?
options: A permission that remains assigned to a user or service account after it is no longer needed, such as a departed employee's unremoved account
A log file that has expired and can no longer be retrieved
An encryption key that has passed its rotation schedule
A password that has not been changed recently
questions.explain: Stale access is a permission left in place after it's no longer needed — a classic example is an ex-employee's account that was never disabled, or a one-time admin role never revoked.

questions.q: Why is "missing logging" considered one of the most common real audit findings?
options: Logging disabled on a resource, or retention set shorter than the audit period, leaves no evidence trail for the window an auditor actually needs to review
Auditors never actually check whether logging is enabled
Logging is optional under every compliance framework, so it is never flagged
Missing logging only matters for on-premises systems, not cloud environments
questions.explain: If logging is disabled or its retention period is too short to cover the audit window, there is no record to show an auditor for that period — a gap that is easy to miss until fieldwork begins.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the benefit of running tools like Purview Compliance Manager or AWS Audit Manager weeks before an audit rather than during it?
options: They surface gaps like stale access or missing logging while there's still time to actually fix them, instead of discovering them live during the real audit
They automatically pass the audit without any human review
They are only useful after the audit has already concluded
They replace the need for any written policy documents
questions.explain: Running these tools ahead of fieldwork surfaces exactly the kinds of gaps auditors flag, giving a team time to remediate them before the real audit instead of being caught by surprise.
